clue.text: Wily uncle of Chaucer, and a spur, oddly enough

indicators.note: something done oddly is done in a strange way, so these letters are put into a strange new order

explanation.surface: A scheming relative of the poet is compared, oddly, to a riding spur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' turns AND A SPUR into the answer. Pandarus is the go-between uncle of Criseyde in Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde.
explanation.definitionFit: In Chaucer's Troilus poem the crafty go-between who arranges the lovers' meeting is Criseyde's uncle, the figure whose name gave us 'pander'.

clue.text: Gap pair contrived to discover Roman commander

indicators.note: contrived means artificially arranged, so these letters are rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: A mismatched couple is engineered so as to uncover an ancient general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrived' rearranges GAP PAIR. Marcus Agrippa was Augustus's admiral and general, victor at Actium.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa led Octavian's fleet at Actium, a famous military leader of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Jacobean sleuth, so to speak

parts.note: Jacobean normally means of the reign of James I; here, playfully, it means belonging to the novelist P. D. James, whose detective is a Scotland Yard poet-policeman

explanation.surface: A detective from the age of King James I, after a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jacobean' looks like a period label but means 'of P. D. James', the crime novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam, the Scotland Yard commander who solves P. D. James's murders, is that novelist's series detective.

clue.text: Bad lot included in Cleopatra's, Calpurnia's and Julia's acquaintance

indicators.note: included in means the letters sit inside the run of Roman women's names that follows

explanation.surface: A scoundrel is counted among the friends of three famous Roman women.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of CleopatRA'S and the start of CALpurnia's; Julia's is decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad lot is a rogue or scamp, a person of poor character.

clue.text: Seasonable illumination shed by Wodehouse

parts.note: a flash in the sky typical of the warm season, and also the title of a Blandings Castle novel by P. G. Wodehouse

explanation.surface: Light appropriate to the time of year, cast by a comic novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Wodehouse's 1929 Blandings novel takes its title from the silent sheet flashes seen on warm nights.

clue.text: Origin of word in Society (monthly publication)

indicators.note: in tells us the letters are sitting inside the words Society and monthly

explanation.surface: A word's source appears in a learned society's monthly journal.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters bridge sociETY and MONthly; 'publication' only completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymon is the root form from which a later word derives, its linguistic source.

clue.text: Dye Curie prepared for friend of lyrist

indicators.note: prepared suggests something made up or mixed, so these letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A colouring agent concocted by the physicist Marie Curie for a singer's companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges DYE CURIE. The lyrist is Orpheus, who played the lyre and went to the underworld for his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpheus the lyre-player loved and lost the nymph he tried to lead back from Hades, so she is his beloved.

clue.text: Souvenir chaps found in damaged tome

indicators.note: found in means one piece is located inside the other
damaged means the word tome is knocked out of shape, its letters reordered

parts.note: chaps means men

explanation.surface: Some fellows discover a keepsake inside a battered old book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' rearranges the letters of 'tome' to METO; 'found in' then signals that 'chaps' sits inside that result.
explanation.definitionFit: A memento is a keepsake kept to recall a person or event.

clue.text: A passage from Kenneth Roberts

parts.note: not an extract from his prose but the title of his 1937 historical novel about Rogers' Rangers, named after the Arctic sea route

explanation.surface: An excerpt quoted from the American novelist Kenneth Roberts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passage' suggests a quoted extract; it is the title of Roberts's novel, itself named for the Arctic sea route.
explanation.definitionFit: Roberts's best-known novel takes its title from the fabled Arctic sea route sought between Atlantic and Pacific.

clue.text: Fishes for mythical cave-dwellers

explanation.surface: Someone angles for the creatures of Norse legend that live in caves.
explanation.definitionFit: To troll is to fish by trailing a line behind a boat; Scandinavian folklore's ugly giants live under bridges and in caves.

clue.text: Known as a writer/barrister but Marlowe's was younger

explanation.surface: A man famed as both author and lawyer, though the Elizabethan playwright's version was a youth.
explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer wrote the Rumpole stories and was a barrister; Marlowe's Edward II has a character called Mortimer Junior.
explanation.definitionFit: John, the Rumpole author, practised at the bar; Marlowe's Edward II features the younger Roger of that name.

clue.text: Betting system the Italian way suggested by crime writer

parts.note: SP is starting price, the odds system used in British horse-race betting
il is the Italian word for 'the'
a lane is a way or road

explanation.surface: A gambling method done the way they do it in Italy, proposed by a thriller author.
explanation.walkthrough: SP is 'starting price', the odds a British bookmaker pays on a horse at the off.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickey, creator of Mike Hammer, wrote hard-boiled detective thrillers.

clue.text: "Guido… shook off the relics of his poison — " (Browning, The Ring and the Book)

definitions.text: "Guido… shook off the relics of his poison — " (Browning, The Ring and the Book)

parts.words: "Guido… shook off the relics of his poison — " (Browning, The Ring and the Book)
parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing: the solver supplies the word that completes Browning's line, a dose of liquid

explanation.surface: A line from Browning's long poem about a Roman murder trial, its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word follows 'poison-' in the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage a drench is a draught or dose of medicine or poison, still the word for a dose given to livestock.

clue.text: Isabella's potherb

parts.note: in Keats's poem Isabella, or the Pot of ... she buries her murdered lover's head in a garden pot and grows a herb over it

explanation.surface: The kitchen herb belonging to a woman called Isabella.
explanation.walkthrough: Isabella is Keats's heroine, who hides Lorenzo's head in a pot of this herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's subtitle names the sweet herb she grows in the pot over her lover's head.

clue.text: He was seen in the Savoy wih Conrad

definitions.text: He was seen in the Savoy wih Conrad

parts.words: He was seen in the Savoy wih Conrad
parts.note: the Savoy here is not the London hotel but the 1890s art magazine, whose art editor's drawings appeared alongside Conrad's fiction

explanation.surface: A man was spotted at the grand London hotel with the novelist Joseph Conrad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Savoy' suggests the hotel; it is the 1896 magazine The Savoy, where Aubrey's drawings and Conrad's story 'The Idiots' appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey, the decadent illustrator, was art editor of The Savoy magazine, which also printed Conrad.

clue.text: Known as a writer/barrister and, secondarily, to be in want of what O. Twist demanded

parts.note: B is the conventional letter for second place or second class
to lack is to be in want of
Oliver Twist famously asked the workhouse master for more

explanation.surface: A man famed as author and lawyer also, in a minor way, wants what the workhouse orphan begged for.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist asks 'Please, sir, I want some more' in Dickens's novel. R. D. Blackmore, author of Lorna Doone, trained as a barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: R. D., author of Lorna Doone, was called to the bar before turning novelist.

clue.text: Notes on war by author of Passage to India

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Notes on war by author of Passage to India (9)'; no parse found for MEMORANDA: 'Notes' defines it, but 'on war by author of Passage to India' (perhaps MORAND, of La Route des Indes) leaves ME and A unaccounted for and 'war' unused
annotationWithheld.clue: Notes on war by author of Passage to India

clue.text: Strange legacies of mournful couplets

indicators.note: strange means odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters of legacies are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Odd bequests consisting of sorrowful verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges LEGACIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Elegiac verse alternates hexameter and pentameter lines in pairs, the classical metre for laments.

clue.text: From Greece, a bouquet of verse, perhaps

definitions.text: From Greece, a bouquet of verse, perhaps

parts.words: From Greece, a bouquet of verse, perhaps
parts.note: the Greek source word means a gathering of flowers, and a collection of poems is figuratively such a posy

explanation.surface: A bunch of flowers sent from Greece, perhaps made of poems.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek root means 'flower-gathering'; the Greek Anthology is also a famous collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A compiled collection of poems, its Greek root meaning a gathering of blossoms.

clue.text: Where to see matinée at three approximately

indicators.note: approximately means roughly, so the letters of at three are only roughly in order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice on where to catch an afternoon show starting around three o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'approximately' rearranges AT THREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinée is an afternoon performance, staged in a playhouse.

clue.text: Scope found in Lamb, it seems

indicators.note: found in means the letters lie inside the words Lamb and it

explanation.surface: Range is discovered in the essayist Charles Lamb, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters bridge lAMB and IT; Lamb looks like the essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambit is the extent or range of something's influence.

clue.text: Object of illuminating work in early book

definitions.text: Object of illuminating work in early book

parts.words: Object of illuminating work in early book
parts.note: medieval scribes decorated the large opening letter of a page or chapter in gold and colour; also 'early' alone means first

explanation.surface: Something a medieval scribe decorated in an ancient manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: 'illuminating' is manuscript decoration, not shedding light; such large decorated opening letters begin early books.
explanation.definitionFit: Illuminators lavished gilding on the big capital opening a manuscript page, and the word also means first or opening.

clue.text: Delete a few notes on Ben Jonson's housekeeper, Jeremy

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first piece sits on top of the next

parts.note: E and F are two musical notes
in Jonson's The Alchemist, Jeremy the butler left in charge of Lovewit's house goes by the alias Face

explanation.surface: Remove a few musical notes written about the servant in a Jacobean comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Alchemist, Jeremy, the servant keeping his master's house, poses as Captain Face.
explanation.definitionFit: To efface is to rub out or erase, wiping something from view.

clue.text: Product of the hand of Auden's colourist?

definitions.text: Product of the hand of Auden's colourist?

parts.words: Product of the hand of Auden's colourist?
parts.note: Auden's essay collection is The Dyer's Hand; what a colourist's hand produces is the act of colouring cloth

explanation.surface: What the hand of a painter friend of the poet produced.
explanation.walkthrough: Auden's prose book The Dyer's Hand supplies the joke: the dyer's hand produces this.
explanation.definitionFit: Colouring fabric with stain is what a dyer's hand does.

clue.text: Stern guard for Captain Dorling

explanation.surface: A rear protector working for a naval officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Henry Taprell Dorling wrote naval stories under this pen name.
explanation.definitionFit: The rail round a ship's stern guards the poop deck, and Captain Dorling wrote naval fiction under that nautical pen name.

clue.text: Latin writers, and others

parts.note: the Latin plural for lettered people, used in English for the learned class of any nation

explanation.surface: Roman authors, plus a few more besides.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself a Latin word, and covers the learned of any nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the Latin plural for educated, bookish people, borrowed for intellectuals generally.

clue.text: Irish poet with Northeastern identity produces epic

parts.note: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell
NE is the abbreviation for northeast
ID is short for identity

explanation.surface: An Irish versifier with a north-eastern background creates a heroic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: AE was the pseudonym of George Russell, Irish poet of the Celtic revival.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's poem of Aeneas is the great Latin heroic narrative poem.

clue.text: "That … woods or steepy mountain — " (Marlowe)

parts.note: a quotation with its last word missing, from The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, where valleys, groves, hills and fields offer up pleasures

explanation.surface: A line from Marlowe's pastoral love poem, its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank: 'That valleys, groves, hills, and fields, Woods, or steepy mountain ...'
explanation.definitionFit: The landscape gives forth pleasures, so the verb means produces or affords.

clue.text: Historian offers excerpt from fugue Dallapiccola wrote

indicators.note: an excerpt is a piece taken from a longer work, so the letters are lifted from inside these words

explanation.surface: A scholar presents a passage from a fugue by the Italian composer Dallapiccola.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters bridge fuGUE and DALLApiccola. Philip Guedalla was a popular British historian and biographer.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Guedalla wrote popular histories and biographies such as The Second Empire.
